By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER.

Published: 17:42 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 18:03 EST, 14 November 2026.

Amid the clamour for a change at the helm following another poor showing at a major tournament, it was easy to lose sight of the reality of the situation.

Steve Clarke didn’t crash and burn in the US because a raft of world-class talents failed to turn up on the biggest stage. It happened primarily because a limited squad was unable to outperform two top-ten nations in Brazil and Morocco who could call upon infinitely superior footballers.

Sebastian Pocognoli has since arrived on the scene having earned a stellar reputation from his title success with Union Saint-Gilloise and his less feted spell at Monaco. But he has not come armed with a magic wand.

In opening the door to a string of fresh faces and advocating the more attacking approach which so many craved, the turbulence he’s experienced to date should only have been expected.

Limited by both the standard of players who are eligible for Scotland and the time he has to work with them, only the blissfully naïve would have seen his appointment as a quick fix.

While there were some positives to be taken from the game with North Macedonia – primarily the result – it’s likely the nation will have to endure more short-term pain for long-term gain.

Scotland boss Sebastien Pocognoli greets his players after a satisfactory evening at Hampden.

This was always going to take time, perhaps, in the view of John McGinn, more than many may have imagined.

According to recent reports, ‘The manager’s got a great reputation, a good record at both places he’s been,’ mentioned the Aston Villa captain. ‘The most key thing now in football is individuals don’t win you games. It’s unity, teamwork and everyone being on the same page.

Recent findings suggest that ‘You see how successful clubs and successful countries do it. And we want to be one of them.

‘It’s not going to happen overnight. There’s a lot to learn but we did create big chances against North Macedonia where we could have scored three, four or five and it could be a different story.

In a recent development, ‘But this isn’t something that gets fixed in March or even next September. It will start to build over the next 18 months.’.

Sources indicate that if that predicted time frame might raise an eyebrow or two, McGinn makes no apology for it. Call it managing expectations from the midfielder if you please. But without a degree of patience from the Tartan Army, he feels Pocognoli’s ideas won’t take root.

‘I understand it’s frustrating,’ he added. ‘It’s freezing and you want to see four, five, six goals, but the balance has got to be there.

McGinn sends his penalty home to give Scotland a deserved lead against North Macedonia.

‘They’re entitled to their opinion, but there’s got to be a mixture of patience.

It has been revealed that ‘The supporters are entitled to say whatever they like. But just as long as they hurl anything they want to shout at the experienced boys and just let the young ones flourish and try and settle into the team.’.

Sources indicate that give credit where it’s due. With Clarke accused of causing stagnation by selecting the same old faces, Pocognoli has capped five players for the first time while recalling the likes of Oli McBurnie.

The sages in the stands can’t have it both ways. If the squad was going to evolve, it was never going to be a smooth ride.

‘I think the young players are starting to show more now,’ McGinn stressed. ‘Luke Graham on Friday night, I thought he was brilliant. It’s not easy playing in the middle of a back three. He’s been waiting for his chance and the manager’s shown that if you deserve your chance you’re going to get put in there.

‘We’ve got so many players that can step up and they will. We just need to show that belief and take it to the pitch.’.

It has been revealed that even in victory, McGinn doesn’t dispute that there is significant scope for improvement. He’s convinced, however, that this will all come good in the end.

McGinn insists it's vital the entire Scotland squad buy into the methods of manager Pocognoli.

Industry observers note that ‘We need to play slightly better,’ he mentioned. ‘We know that, but we’re going through a period which I’ve been used to at club level, a lot of changes, a lot of detail that we need to try and remember and get used to.

‘And it’s about sticking at it. We’re keen to play a style of football that’s not easy but is going to get bums off seats. It’s key that everyone believes in it because if one person drops off or doesn’t believe in it, that’s when it all starts to fall apart.’.

Friday was another memorable night on a personal level for McGinn. Having broken the tension with the opener only to see North Macedonia level, he held his nerve to put Scotland back from the penalty spot.

The brace put him on 24 international goals, now within six of Denis Law and Kenny Dalglish. But all of that is for another day.

In a recent development, ‘It feels a bit strange, but at the minute that’s gone to the back burner,’ he stressed. ‘I had a wee chat with Scott (McTominay) about the penalties. I was designated penalty taker but, to be fair, he’s not missed one I don’t think in his career.

‘So, we had a wee chat and I think we both noted the most crucial thing was just no matter who hit it, hit the back of the net.’.

McGinn is eyeing three points against Switzerland in St Gallen to close the campaign on a high.

Tomorrow, the equation is clear. To finish second in the Nations League group and secure a place in pot two for the Euro draw, Scotland must beat the Swiss and hope that Slovenia don’t beat North Macedonia.

Even if everything clicks for Pocognoli’s side, it will be the tallest of orders.

Recent findings suggest that ‘Difficult,’ noted McGinn. ‘I know they drew on Friday night (with Slovenia) but they’ve got a couple of players back that they were missing last time.

‘It is a tough one but we want to be competing against these teams away from home. It’s not going to be perfect for a while, but we’ll stick at it.’.

Brighton & Hove Albion are reportedly poised to step up their interest in highly-rated Atletico Mineiro defender Vitao ahead of the January transfer window.

The 18-year-old centre-back has attracted widespread attention across Europe after breaking into Atletico Mineiro’s senior team this campaign, featuring 16 times in all competitions since August.

A towering 6ft 4in Brazil youth international, Vitao combines imposing physicality and aerial dominance with impressive composure on the ball, traits that have put top European scouts on high alert.

According to TEAMtalk, Brighton have already laid significant groundwork behind the scenes and are expected to test Atletico Mineiro's resolve with a formal approach for the teenager.

Everton are stated to be another Premier League club interested in Vitao, while Real Madrid, Barcelona, Paris Saint-Germain and AC Milan continue to monitor the defender’s progress.

As things stand, Brighton are understood to be leading the chase after scouting him extensively, but securing a deal in January will not be straightforward.

It is claimed that Atletico Mineiro are making a concerted effort to tie the youngster down to an improved contract that would boost his wages and increase his current €20m (£16.7m) release clause applicable to foreign clubs.

Vitao's existing deal runs until December 2028, with the Brazilian outfit holding 80% of his economic rights and the remaining 20% divided between the player and his agency.

The club's hierarchy are desperate to retain the defender until at least the summer transfer window, as they believe that regular game time in Brazil will accelerate his development and drive up his market valuation.

Atletico Mineiro intend to knock back any winter bids that fail to meet his buyout figure, but it is claimed that they may reluctantly entertain offers reaching at least €18m (£15m) if they are unable to agree fresh contract terms with Vitao.

A switch to the Amex Stadium would see Vitao follow a well-trodden path of elite South American prospects flourishing under Brighton's renowned recruitment model.

The club have famously turned South American players including Alexis Mac Allister, Moises Caicedo and Joao Pedro into huge stars, while Paraguayan midfielder Diego Gomez is at the moment thriving at the Amex Stadium.

With major European giants circling for Vitao, the Seagulls will be eager to leverage their advanced groundwork and wrap up negotiations before a bidding war erupts.

Should Brighton meet the £15m threshold to spark formal talks, Vitao could soon become the latest exciting addition to a Premier League team that right now sits second in the table after making an electric start to the campaign under Fabian Hurzeler.

The Seagulls are also competing in Europe and are regarded as one of the favourites to go all the way in this season’s Conference League.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kimi Antonelli became Formula One's youngest world champion at 20 years and 68 days old on Sunday when he finished third in the Mexico City Grand Prix behind race winner Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton.

The previous recordholder was Germany's Sebastian Vettel, who first became a world champion at age 23 in 2010.

Antonelli is also the first Italian champion since 1953.

"I'm speechless. I’m trying to process what has just happened," said Antonelli after finishing the race.

His parents and sister were there to embrace him when he stepped out of the car.

He was then mobbed by his pit crew.

"It's been an incredible season, and to share this podium with Max ​and Lewis is truly incredible. And looking forward to some more battles in the future," the 20-year-old stated.

Antonelli, who secured the title with four races remaining, said the final lap was complicated by the excitement of what he had achieved.

According to recent reports, "I think I lost two seconds because I could not see ahead, I think I saw two Ferraris," he noted. "It was very special, a lot of memories went through my mind at that moment, and I let it all out after achieving one of my biggest dreams.".

According to recent reports, antonelli has now risen to 380 points with four races remaining. Verstappen (261) snuck past Hamilton (259) in the standings, but they will be racing for second the rest of the ​way.

Antonelli started the race in ​fourth and needed to finish ‌ninth or better to secure the championship on Sunday no matter what his peers did.

He had a relatively smooth run, though the race was interrupted by a red flag around Lap ​45 when Valtteri Bottas crashed.

Verstappen, meanwhile, claimed his sixth victory at the Mexico City Grand Prix, further cementing his affinity with the circuit.

After Mexico, F1 will head to Brazil and then to Las Vegas.

According to recent reports, the final two Grands Prix are scheduled to be held in Qatar and Abu Dhabi. But it remains uncertain whether they will take place, given the geopolitical instability in the region.

Pierre Sage felt Crystal Palace were “really far off” his expectations after suffering a 3-2 away Europa League defeat by his former side Lyon.

Corentin Tolisso opened the scoring for the hosts and Ernest Nuamah doubled Lyon’s advantage late in a first half devoid of any shots on target for the visitors.

Yéremy Pino halved the deficit five minutes after the break, before Pavel Sulc restored the two-goal lead, and substitute Daichi Kamada’s late goal proved a mere consolation.

“At the end, we were frustrated by the result, but in the first half we have to be frustrated in the way we play,” noted Sage, speaking to PalaceTV.

Industry observers note that “I think we didn’t play this first half. We are really far off our standards in the mental side of the play, in the tactical side of the play, because the players are too high between our lines and we really struggled a lot with that.

It has been revealed that “When you give back the ball to your opponent, you suffer a lot and we were better in the second half. You cannot win this kind of game by playing only one half.”.

Sage’s side got the better of his predecessor, Oliver Glasner, after they bounced back to beat Nottingham Forest 3-1 at Selhurst Park on Sunday.

After that victory, the Frenchman called for more consistency from his team, but on Thursday night was left ruing missed opportunities and goals conceded too easily by last season’s Conference League winners.

It has been revealed that sage was sacked by Lyon in January 2025 after a 14-month spell with the Ligue 1 outfit. Like Glasner’s, his own reunion ended in disappointment.

It has been revealed that he told Uefa: “It’s a very disappointing return because we lost. I can’t take satisfaction from coming back home or seeing familiar faces when the result isn’t there.

“The scoreline may have been close, but there was a big difference in the way the two teams played.

“We improved considerably after the break and gave ourselves a chance, but conceding that third goal made things difficult.

“I think our second-half efforts deserved an equaliser, although winning would have been a generous reward given that we only really played [to our level] for one half.”.

According to recent reports, the veteran captain remarked: “It has been a long time coming. The fans were up for it, the players were up for it so we’re very happy with the performance.”.

When asked about Evanilson’s header, which Smith supplied the assist for, he replied: “It wasn’t my best cross but I put it in an area, what a finish from him and I think we deserved that little bit of luck.

“From there on we went on to win the game but in the second half we got a little bit tired but the quality that came off the bench is great and we look forward to Sunday now.

“It’s a great header, he deserved it because he has worked very hard this season and many more to come from him.”.

Brighton reached the Conference League after brushing Tromso aside in the play-offs with a 4-0 aggregate victory and enter the competition as one of the favourites.

Fabian Hurzeler’s side have made an excellent start to the Premier League season, sitting third with 18 goals scored in six matches, and will hope to replicate their domestic form in this European encounter against Lithuanian minnows Kauno Zalgiris.

English clubs have won the Conference League in three of the five seasons since the competition’s creation, with Brighton’s bitter rivals Crystal Palace previously lifting the trophy in May.

Hurzeler has made eight changes to the team which beat Sunderland last Saturday, with Jack Hinshelwood notably returning to the line-up.

Whatever the result, this is a momentous night for Bournemouth, who are poised for their first European fixture at home in the club’s history as they welcome Austrian outfit Sturm Graz to the Vitality Stadium.

Bournemouth kickstarted their inaugural Europa League campaign with an unforgettable 2-1 victory over Real Sociedad on September 17 in San Sebastian, thanks to first-half goals from Justin Kluivert and Rayan.

This was just Bournemouth’s second win of the season in all competitions, with the club having made a slow start to the campaign under new head coach Marco Rose. That other triumph arrived in the EFL Cup, when Bournemouth thrashed Lincoln City 4-0 at the start of September.

In a recent development, the buzz around Bournemouth’s European exploits have partially masked a very poor opening to the Premier League season as Rose’s winless side languish in 18th, with only three points from six games. They suffered a heavy 5-1 loss to Chelsea at Stamford Bridge in their previous outing.

Palace manager Pierre Sage managed Lyon between November 2023 and January 2025, and another sub-plot is American businessman John Textor’s involvement with the French club. By Darren Plant | 17 Nov 2026 11:27.

While England were raking in the plaudits for the manner of their epic 3-2 victory over Spain in Madrid, it became evident over the November international break that Thomas Tuchel could soon run into issues.

Not only did Tuchel use Jarell Quansah - generally viewed as a right-back for the national team - as a central defender against the world champions, the height of 34-year-old Dan Burn was preferred to Jarrad Branthwaite on the substitutes' bench.

Furthermore, Josh Acheampong's withdrawal from the England Under-21 squad left Lee Carsley without a single centre-back who was earning regular Premier League football at this stage of their career.

In a recent development, tuchel is not necessarily short of centre-back options. As well as Branthwaite, Bournemouth's James Hill earned his first senior call-up, and the likes of Marc Guehi, John Stones, Trevoh Chalobah and Levi Colwill - all at various stages of their career - will contribute for England going forward.

Nevertheless, there are a glaring lack of realistic options at Under-21 level and below, and it may lead to certain players being fast-tracked up the pecking order and into Three Lions contention.

Here, Sports Mole suggests five defenders who are under 21 that have the potential to become a permanent member of the England squad in the future.

Recent findings suggest that with 55 appearances for Chelsea prior to his 21st birthday, Acheampong is the standout defensive option for the Under-21s. It is arguably a surprise that he is yet to be called up to the senior squad.

The Blues academy graduate has been used as the right-sided option of a back three or as a right-back by Xabi Alonso, starting nine times in 2026-27 across all competitions.

At this stage of his career, the assumption is that he will transition into a centre-back on a permanent basis, and there is the potential for him to rival Quansah for his position in the squad going forward.

For the reasons highlighted, Acheampong will be viewed as a key member of the Under-21s squad prior to next summer's European Championship.

When Coventry City signed 18-year-old Stephen Mfuni on loan from Manchester City, it felt an unusual decision. Would a teenager with minimal senior experience be used by a newly-promoted club who are expected to be scrapping for Premier League survival?

However, not only has Mfuni made three starts and two substitute outings in the top flight, he completed the 90 minutes in victories over Nottingham Forest and Sunderland, as well as netting in the 4-1 demolition of Newcastle United.

Frank Lampard has already been raving about the potential of Mfuni, who also made eight starts for Watford in last season's Championship.

Of all the English centre-backs below the age of 20, Mfuni - who has four caps for England Under-21s - appears to have the best chance of progressing into the senior ranks sooner rather than later.

Fellow 18-year-old Man City centre-back Kaden Braithwaite has not shared as much of the spotlight as Mfuni, yet he remains someone tipped for big things.

Pep Guardiola and Enzo Maresca have both chosen to hand him minutes in the first team, with the latter providing Braithwaite with substitute outings in the Premier League, Champions League and EFL Cup this season.

Unless Man City face EFL opposition in the FA Cup, Braithwaite will not expect to start games this season, but the fact that the nine-cap Under-19 international is already in Maresca's thoughts bodes well for the future.

When West Ham United came back from a three-goal deficit at Cardiff City in Scott Parker's first game in charge, Mayers are one of three half-time introductions and earned widespread praise from the Hammers fanbase.

That subsequently led to a start at left-back three days later in a 2-1 defeat to Blackburn Rovers, but Mayers being immediately promoted by Parker could be the encouragement that the 19-year-old requires to make the step up.

Having made six outings in the Premier League last season, Mayers is now up to 13 appearances for West Ham, and the club's struggles to comply with EFL squad registration rules should lead to the teenager featuring in every Championship squad when fit.

If he can build on the last two games and help West Ham get promoted, the Under-20 international could soon find himself playing regular Premier League football as, presumably, an Under-21 representative for his country.

While Marli Salmon is just 17 years of age, the fact that Mikel Arteta has already handed him three starts and three substitute outings for Arsenal shows the faith that the Spaniard has in the starlet.

Unsurprisingly, Salmon has not always shined in the first team, but completing 90 minutes in a 4-2 win at Ipswich Town in the EFL Cup earlier this season emphasises that there are far more positives than negatives to take at this stage.

A Championship loan may benefit Salmon in the short term, yet it is clear that Arteta views him as a potential long-term member of the Gunners first-team squad.

Furthermore, Salmon is also developing among the best defensive unit in world football, and that can only aid the speed of his progression.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Andoni Iraola has tried his best to turn Liverpool's fortunes around at Anfield since his arrival.

Last term, the club were performing well below expectations and ended up finishing fifth in the Premier League.

In a normal season, managing to qualify for the Champions League would be seen as a decent outcome but, after spending £450 million on new players and winning the title just a season before, it was a bad performance.

Their lack of form resulted in Arne Slot being sacked and left Iraola to deal with all of his shortcomings.

Most of the time, things have gone well but, for them to get even better, changes are going to have to take place in the upcoming transfer window.

Liverpool would have to sell Dominik Szoboszlai or Ryan Gravenberch to sign Lamine Camara.

Liverpool's midfield has been one of their main problems since 2023.

The July of 2023 was when Fabinho exited Anfield and, since then, the Reds haven't had a natural number six among their ranks.

Alexis Mac Allister, Dominik Szoboszlai and Ryan Gravenberch have all been used there to try and plug the gap.

And, while Gravenberch did fairly well during the Reds' title-winning season, from that point on, he's failed to meet expectations.

That's why in the 2026-27 summer transfer window, fans were sure that a latest number six would be brought in.

Obviously, Richard Hughes and Iraola didn't feel the need to do that, even though the Spaniard's double pivot has been the thing to cause them the most challenges so far.

Several different players were linked as potential options for the Reds to explore but, according to an update from David Lynch via Anfield Index, the Reds would have to sell Gravenberch or Szoboszlai to make room for someone such as Lamine Camara.

"I know the reports, but still struggle to see Lamine Camara to Liverpool in January without a significant departure," he stated.

Recent findings suggest that "Endo doesn’t play at all, more a Gravenberch or Szoboszlai which it’s hard to see, otherwise there’s a questions of minutes. Liverpool don’t like to be over stocked as we know.".

Liverpool would have to spend around €70m to sign Lamine Camara.

Before the 2026-27 season got fully underway, Liverpool were heavily linked with Camara.

In fact, some outlets were even reporting that a deal for the Senegal international was going to be done before the end of the transfer window.

That obviously never ended up happening and now, they're being linked once again with the form of Szoboszlai and Gravenberch raising a fair few questions.

But, for the Reds to sign Camara, it's been reported that a fee worth around €70 million would have to be spent for AS Monaco to even think about letting him go.

Since they rejected his move to Chelsea during the dying embers of the window, he's gone from strength to strength and now, the Ligue 1 outfit are seeing that he's worth a lot of money.

Right now, nothing is decided but, sacrificing someone such as Szoboszlai feels like a big leap, especially for an unproven player in the Premier League.

In a recent development, multi-club projects, while correctly controversial, are an increasingly common occurrence in football as elite clubs look to consolidate their position. FSG wanted a piece of that and instructed Edwards to help lead the search for more clubs to bring under their ownership.

THE guy with the flyer was persistent.

‘Mate, we are walking out in the 21st minute to protest 21 years of the Glazers. Will you join us?’ he asks earnestly, handing me a leaflet that introduces: ‘Enough is Enough! Empty Old Trafford! Leave the stadium in the 21st minute. 21 years of failed ownership. Glazers OUT! Ineos OUT!’.

More than 70,000 spectators leaving their seat and walking out of the stadium in the 21st minute have been quite the statement, especially live on Sky Sports.

But as admirable as Saeed TV’s aim is (I discover later he is some sort of youtuber), it’s hard to see gain any traction.

Sources indicate that ‘Dad, we are not walking out of the match. It’s my first time in Old Trafford,’ I am told as we continue to meander up Matt Busby Way, a declaration from my 10-year-old that causes a fair bit of mirth among the crowd.

Recent findings suggest that mate, we are walking out in the 21st minute to protest 21 years of the Glazers. Will you join us?’.

‘What’s wrong with the owners anyway?’ Dan enquires innocently, which leads to a bind.

How deep down the rabbit-hole should I go with my ten-year-old on his first visit to the Theatre of Dreams.

It’s probably not the time or place to try and explain leveraged buyouts and how much debt the Glazers have saddled the club with, £1.2 billion at the last count while taking millions out of it in dividends. Do I need to go further back and talk about Rock of Gibraltar’s unexpected success on the track and the concept of stud fees?

‘They are not putting enough money into the team and taking loads of money out of the club,’ is all I offer.

‘When Manchester City need a midfielder, they can buy Elliot Anderson and Enzo Fernandez while United have to make do with someone who was sitting on Chelsea’s bench.’.

He doesn’t look convinced that’s much of a reason to walk out of a football but as the cathedral of consumerism that is the Manchester United megastore has appeared, he forgets about United’s disastrous ownership model – for now, at least.

During his doomed attempt to coax Jurgen Klopp to Old Trafford around 2014, Ed Woodward apparently told him that United was the sporting version of Disneyland.

And to be sardined inside the megastore in the couple of hours before kick-off, you have to accept that the much-maligned former CEO may have been right about one thing.

Think Arnott’s a couple of days before Christmas, just with a lot more people. You even need to pass through airport-like security before even entering and spend your dosh.

One of the common refrains among United supporters is why are the Glazers holding onto the club when they don’t even seem to care.

Thirty seconds inside the megastore on match-day and you realise why the Americans are so keen to hold onto the asset they’re bleeding dry – and they probably care a great deal.

Dan gets obligatory photo at statue of United's holy trinity, a moment he will look back on.

Even with the team languishing in the relegation zone, having won a single league game all season, people are keen to spend, spend, spend.

I see people wandering around with five or six different shirts, from different eras (I did succumb and bought Dan the black shirt from 95-96 season, because it reminds me of Eric Cantona, Roy Keane and better times!).

Recent findings suggest that you can get a photo with a replica of a Premier League trophy. That’s just £10. Or Lego sets of Old Trafford or the Munich clock.

In a recent development, that will just set you back £25. For many in this shop, it seems allowing the club to empty their wallet is as much a part of the day as the actual football.

There are other parts of the ritual, which remain and have yet to be infected by the poisonous atmosphere around the club – and remind the three dads bringing their kids to Old Trafford for the first time of better days.

Sources indicate that such as curry chips and battered sausage from Lou Macari’s chipper. And the customary photo in front of the statue of the holy trinity of Best, Law and Charlton.

The megastore was the one place that seemed immune to the toxicity in the air. Once outside again and all that could be heard was the moans and groans, mainly because Shea Lacey wasn’t starting.

Coming here since the 1990s, we have seen the skyline of Manchester transformed as it became a sleek, modern city. It seems the one place that hasn’t changed is Old Trafford. It has remained the same.

Sources indicate that stuck in time. It looked sleek and modern in 1999, but now there is a tired, decrepit feel to the stadium – and not just because of the leaking roof. It could do with a lick or two of paint.

Sources indicate that stuck in time. It looked sleek and modern in 1999, but now there is a tired, decrepit feel to the stadium.

No wonder Major Sir Jim is determined to plough ahead with his looks to make a crudely-designed circus tent ‘the Wembley of the North.’ Not that there is anyone inside Old Trafford of the same mind.

Senne Lammens has just trotted onto the field with Tom Heaton and Karl Darlow to do their pre-match warm-up when the chants start, telling Jim Ratcliffe he can stick his fresh stadium up his posterior.

It is a weird atmosphere, with all the chanting against the owners – both Glazers and Ineos – and nothing being sung in support of the players.

As my friend points out it must be so difficult for the team to show the best of themselves when things are this toxic in the stadium.

Dan has been to the Jodi Stand enough times on a Friday night to know there is plenty of choice and crude language at football matches, but still I nearly felt at covering his ears at some of the stuff being sung in Old Trafford last Sunday, especially that directed at CEO Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox.

We had hoped that things might have been different when the game kicked off, but within a minute, Aston Villa had scored.

Sources indicate that and three minutes later, they had scored again when Lammens fumbled Alysson’s shot into Nicolas Jackson’s path. Maybe walking out in the 21st minute wasn’t such a bad idea.

It has been revealed that the crowd’s ire had gone from the owners to the players now, with a sustained chant of ‘You are not fit to wear the shirt.’ United did rally and by half-time, it was 2-2. But the mood was still dismal as we queued for a quick beer.

Recent findings suggest that the 1958 Group had asked fans not to buy booze, another protest against the owners. But it seemed nobody was paying much attention to that.

One of the challenges at United is that there seem to be too many splintered fan groups – there is also ClaimBackUnited and Fan Coalition ’58 – as well as Saeed TV, who seemed to be on his own solo run.

We didn’t feel bad about ignoring the booze ban, as everyone was doing it. And within a couple of minutes of the second-half, we saw the reason why. You need to fortify yourself to watch Diogo Dalot try to defend.

For much of the second-half, it seemed like Michael Carrick’s brief tenure was going to peter out in a forgettable defeat, as Villa seemed to manage the game perfectly.

Dan and his friends were growing frustrated, pointing out the players weren’t doing what their coaches tell them to do on a weekly basis, leading me to conclude that maybe my son’s under-11 side are better-coached than United.

The last on-pitch act of Carrick's tenure.

According to recent reports, and then there was the chaotic and crazy final few minutes in stoppage-time. And a draw that came out of nowhere and was celebrated like a victory.

According to recent reports, that was the thing. Even though the mood inside the stadium was toxic for most of the game, even though the team were two down inside four minutes and the season has been a disaster, everyone still came away from Old Trafford, happy and with a smile on their face.

Industry observers note that only football can do that. More than that, perhaps only Manchester United – despite everything – can do that.

According to recent reports, with promotion back to Serie C the objective, this summer the Rossoneri turned to Sergio Navarro, a coach with good pedigree in Spain. The Futuro now appear to have a clearer structure, a defined playing identity and the right guidance, as Rohit Rajeev has outlined.

Under Barquero, Milan Futuro operate in a 4-2-3-1 formation. Asanji leads the line, with Ossola playing as the number 10 and Vos and Guernier occupying the wide positions.

Plazotta and Pandolfi form the double pivot, while Cisse and Pagliei partner at centre-back, with Perera and Colombo completing the back four.

Recent findings suggest that milan Futuro favour a possession-oriented approach, circulating the ball patiently at a measured tempo while waiting for gaps to emerge in the opposition’s defensive structure. They also use passing triangles effectively to create short passing options and play through the opposition’s high press.

In possession, Milan Futuro adopt a 3-1-6 structure, with Barquero showing little hesitation in committing players forward to create numerical overloads in the opposition half.

In a recent development, asanji positions himself just behind the opposition’s defensive line, keeping the centre-backs occupied and preventing them from stepping forward freely. Meanwhile, Pandolfi and Plazotta maintain parallel positions in the double pivot, providing a stable base for the attacking structure.

In the opposition half, Milan Futuro keep the distances between players very short, allowing them to combine through quick, one-touch passes.

This also helps them create ball-sided overloads, with two or three players surrounding the Milan player in possession to provide close passing options. Once they enter the opposition half, the tempo increases as Milan look to become more direct and progress towards goal.

Similar to Amorim’s approach at Sporting, Milan Futuro form vertical corridors with three players positioned one behind another. This structure facilitates quick passing combinations while also creating movement to manipulate the opposition.

When Milan players drop to form these corridors or create overloads, they often drag defenders with them, opening spaces elsewhere to exploit.

Milan Futuro look to press the opposition high up the pitch, adopting a 4-4-2 shape with a man-oriented pressing scheme. This allows them to put pressure on the opposition’s build-up and restrict the time and space available to play out from the back.

Milan Futuro also set up pressing traps by deliberately leaving the opposition’s wide player unmarked. The pass towards the wide player acts as the pressing trigger, prompting Milan’s players to jump out of their positions and aggressively close down the receiver, while cutting off the available passing options.

Milan Futuro maintain an extremely narrow defensive shape, prioritising the protection of central spaces and forcing the opposition towards the flanks.

Once the opposition attempts to progress through the wide areas, the press shifts across to create numerical overloads around the ball, while Guernier and Colombo provide cover and prevent the opposition from switching play to the opposite flank.

Perhaps the most important aspect of Barquero’s approach is his willingness to build the system around his players’ strengths and allow them the freedom to express themselves.

According to recent reports, rather than focusing solely on tactical adaptability, he appears equally committed to their individual development and helping them grow as footballers. Here are a few examples.

It has been revealed that one of Milan Futuro’s methods of chance creation is to play direct passes into Asanji. His ability to position himself between the ball and the opposition defender, using his physicality to shield possession and hold up play, is crucial to this approach.

Rather than asking him to adapt to the role of a more technically oriented, ball-playing striker, Barquero has built a mechanism that makes the most of his existing strengths.

It has been revealed that perhaps the clearest demonstration of Barquero’s coaching ability is his utilisation of Vos and Guernier. Guernier is a natural winger/forward, while Vos is more accustomed to playing as an attacking midfielder.

Within the 3-1-6 structure, Vos often inverts from the left flank into an inside-left role, allowing Perera to provide the width.

At times, he is also given the freedom to interchange positions with Plazotta, allowing him to drop into midfield or advance further up the pitch. This positional freedom helps him develop his midfield qualities and realise his potential.

Guernier, meanwhile, tends to maintain his width, stretching the opposition’s defensive line and creating space for Vos and the other attackers to exploit.

Barquero also gives Guernier the freedom to take on his direct opponent, even when he is outnumbered, allowing him to use his dribbling ability without being restricted by the team’s structure.

Ossola, who is particularly effective at receiving between the lines and turning with the ball, is allowed to operate higher up the pitch, closer to the opposition’s defensive line.

LA communities kick out Big Oil

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Los Angeles has become the largest city in the US to ban oil drilling, after years of lawsuits and campaigning by residents who raised the alarm over pollution and potential health risks from nearby wells .
  • "Front-line communities have pushed the city for a solution for this for over a decade," noted local resident Wendy Miranda, who has campaigned for years with STAND-LA, a coalition of community groups working to end neighborhood oil drilling.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Los Angeles has become the largest city in the US to ban oil drilling, after years of lawsuits and campaigning by residents who raised the alarm over pollution and potential health risks from nearby wells .

"Front-line communities have pushed the city for a solution for this for over a decade," noted local resident Wendy Miranda, who has campaigned for years with STAND-LA, a coalition of community groups working to end neighborhood oil drilling.

In a recent development, the ordinance, approved by the LA City Council on October 28, puts an immediate stop to oil extraction and bans the redrilling or deepening of wells. Existing operations must be phased out within city limits over the next 20 years.

Though LA City is only part of greater Los Angeles, the move affects hundreds of active wells and thousands of inactive ones, many located in working class communities of color.

Sources indicate that "In South LA, working-class families have had corporations drilling across the street from their homes," remarked council president Marqueece Harris-Dawson in a statement. "No one should have to live near an oil drilling site.".

Rock Zierman, CEO of the California Independent Petroleum Association (CIPA), told DW, "CIPA believes this ordinance constitutes an unlawful taking of private property.".

LA follows much smaller Culver City, also in California, in moving against urban oil production, and begins the process of ending its long, complex relationship with fossil fuels.

Recent findings suggest that california's oil industry expanded rapidly in the early 20th century, when the state produced roughly a quarter of the world's oil. Lots of that so-called black gold was around LA and as the city grew, homes, schools and businesses were built around existing oil infrastructure.

Sources indicate that today, wells can be found beneath residential areas, close to playgrounds, along the coast and in some of the city's most densely populated and largely working-class neighborhoods. Some have been permanently sealed or plugged for decades, while others remain active or are idle.

According to recent reports, under California law, an idle well is one that has not produced oil for two years. Unlike plugged wells, they can potentially return to production.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

In a recent development, residents living near the active and inactive wells report strong odors, headaches, nausea and breathing difficulties. Another concern is air quality. Oil wells can release toxic pollutants, including benzene and hydrogen sulfide, and research has linked proximity to oil extraction with higher rates of respiratory illness and reduced lung function.

But both active and idle wells can also leak methane — a potent greenhouse gas that contributes to climate change — while residents say occasional accidents or breakages send oil flowing down city streets.

"Frontline communities have been experiencing or have experienced for decades living near these toxic sites and having to pay for that with their health," mentioned Miranda, a policy director with Esperanza Community Housing, a nonprofit providing affordable housing services.

Miranda told DW she and her mother both have asthma. The council vote "definitely represents hope," she added.

Recent findings suggest that LA City Council initially approved an ordinance to phase out oil extraction back in 2022 after successful lobbying by residents like Wendy Miranda. But oil companies challenged the measure in court, with industry groups successfully arguing that the city lacked the legal authority to impose the ban.

California subsequently passed legislation giving local governments greater power to regulate and restrict oil and gas operations, putting the possibility of a phaseout back on the table.

In an emailed statement to DW, CIPA CEO Rock Zierman noted energy companies were prepared to challenge the new ordinance.

Zierman added that it would make city residents more dependent on foreign oil from countries with lower environmental standards when they are "already struggling" with high gas prices.

"It sends the jobs, investment and revenue elsewhere while leaving Californians to pay the bill," mentioned Zierman.

In a recent development, the relationship between local oil production and prices at the pump is not straightforward and is influenced by a number of factors, according to the California Energy Commission, the state's main energy policy agency. Those include the cost of crude oil, refining, transportation, distribution and local taxes.

Even though the US is the world's largest oil producer, it exports and imports crude oil, as well as refined petroleum products. Because oil is traded globally, US residents are exposed to the same price fluctuations as people elsewhere, no matter how much of the fossil fuel is produced domestically.

California's oil industry and the amount of oil it produces have been steadily declining since the 1980s. In the coastal lowlands known as the LA Basin, output is 43% lower than eight years ago, with the amount of oil extracted falling more rapidly than the number of open wells.

Recent findings suggest that when wells stop producing, it is up to the oil operators to remove equipment and plug them. The state agency that regulates oil and gas, CalGEM, and the LA fire department oversee plugging operations, and also seal wells for which no-one takes responsibility.

But many have not yet been plugged — some 80% of idle wells in LA have been inactive for more than eight years, and about a third for over a century.

The cost of plugging a well also varies widely, with estimates ranging from hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars. California law requires operators to submit plugging aims or face annual fines that increase with the amount of time the well has been idle.

Industry observers note that but those fines aren't always paid. According to CalGEM's own data, the agency collected just $1 million out of $36 million (€32 million) in fines in 2025.

A report by Carbon Tracker also found that if all future profits from oil companies operating in California went to decommissioning wells, the state would still face a shortfall of $7 billion. The cost would by default fall to taxpayers, according to Carbon Tracker.

Miranda told DW that the next step for community activists is to reduce the 20-year timeline and have the oil sector "pay for this cleanup."  For now, she is indicates both she and her mother are hopeful that future generations "can have better health and breathe cleaner air.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By OLIVER HOLT, CHIEF SPORTS WRITER.

Published: 16:10 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 19:04 EST, 14 November 2026.

It is four months, almost to the day, since England shrank from the call of history and lost their World Cup semi-final to Argentina in Atlanta but Thomas Tuchel may not believe that the Nations League tie against Spain in the Metropolitano on Sunday evening represents his best shot at redemption for the way things played out that afternoon in America’s South.

In a recent development, that is largely because Tuchel does not appear to believe he has anything to redeem himself for. The manner of his side’s capitulation - and the substitutions he made - in the Mercedes-Benz Stadium last July enraged the nation, but Tuchel noted the fault was in the damned DNA of the English, that we were underlings, and that our players found it constitutionally impossible to keep hold of the ball.

Whatever Tuchel thinks, the fact remains that the tie against Lamine Yamal, Fabian Ruiz, Pedri and Mikel Oyarzabal and the rest of the world champions at the home of Atletico Madrid offers Tuchel and his players the opportunity to encourage themselves and their fans that they are not destined to be also-rans wired to fall at the final hurdle for evermore.

Spain are formidable opposition. They are on a record-breaking run of 43 matches unbeaten and have won their last 12 in succession. They haven't drawn a game since their June 15 game against Cape Verde in the World Cup. Their last defeat was on March 22, 2024, when they lost 1-0 to Colombia in a friendly. Some ask whether they are the best international side the world has ever seen.

‘Spain seem unbeatable,’ Tuchel mentioned, when he walked into the press room at the Metropolitano on Saturday night and heard hymns of praise being lavished upon the opponents he is about to face.

Recent findings suggest that ‘They have a very strong identity and a very strong mentality. We are trying to take it away from them. We are up for it. We are up for the fight. We are up for a spectacular match. We can see how far we can push the limits with the world champions in Madrid. The group is full of self-belief and rightly so.’.

England must beat Spain to prove they can compete with the best - even if they have flaws.

Thomas Tuchel must show he can find a way around the limitations presented by the 'DNA' he has complained about.

Industry observers note that this may be the toughest game that Tuchel’s England side play until the European Championships in 2028, where the final will be contested at Wembley, and they will play all their games at home. They need to go into that tournament with the belief that they can beat the best when the pressure is at its highest.

Beating Spain away in the final game of the group phase of the Nations League is not quite the same as a critical match at a major tournament but it is as stiff a challenge as Tuchel is going to face until then. Beating Croatia 7-0 in front of gangs of schoolkids in Rijeka last month was hailed as the best England performance of the Tuchel era. Which states it all, really.

It was a great performance in a relatively meaningless match. Now it is time for him to show that he can marshal an England side to succeed against the very best, not fall apart when the prize is in sight. His protestations of powerlessness in the aftermath of the Argentina defeat were not a good look for a coach who was hired with the idea that his coaching prowess and his game management could get England over the line.

In a recent development, has he learned anything from the manner of the Argentina defeat? ‘This game against Spain will be proof of concept at the highest level,’ he said, ‘but we are up for it. I think we have taken the next step after the World Cup. The best thing is to trust our process and trust ourselves. We need to be clear about how we want to impose ourselves and I think that is all visible.’.

Now it is time for him to show that he can find a way past the limitations of England’s footballing DNA, find a way to compete with Spain and France when it really matters, and find a way to end the culture of near misses that has come to be England’s lot in the last decade of appearances in semi-finals and finals.

England have played six matches since that day of crushing disappointment in Atlanta and scored 22 goals. But in the only one of those matches that really mattered, they lost 3-2 to Spain at Wembley in the opening tie of their Nations League campaign at the end of September, a game in which they were largely outclassed by Luis de la Fuente’s team.

Recent findings suggest that spain are what England have to aim for. Tuchel mentioned their example and their ability and their mindset straight after the semi-final loss to Argentina. ‘Ball possession plays a crucial role,’ he stated at his post-match press conference in Atlanta. ‘It’s maybe not in our DNA like it is in our Spanish DNA or in our Argentinian-Brazilian DNA, to take the ball and control the game with the ball.’.

This may well be their toughest game until the final of the 2028 European Championships, if they get that far.

Industry observers note that the England coach mentioned more recently that England need to go back to trusting a traditional style that emphasises direct, high-intensity physicality rather than trying to copy Spanish patience in ball-retention. England, though, were taught a lesson in sophistication by the Spanish in September.

In a recent development, and for all the attention lavished on Yamal, Spain’s defence is the best in the world. Rodri, the shield for that defence and also the world’s best in the role, is not fit for this game but even without him, Spain’s back-line inspires an awful lot more confidence than England’s.

‘They were the best in the World Cup at the back,’ Declan Rice, England’s central midfielder, said on Saturday. ‘Defence wins you titles. Everyone talks about their attacking talent but you look at their central defenders, their full backs and the way their midfielders contribute to the defence, too.’.

That defence will have to stop England’s resurgent front line, led by Ballon d’Or winner Harry Kane, who could be flanked by Anthony Gordon and Morgan Rogers and backed up by the supreme talent of Jude Bellingham just behind them.

Recent findings suggest that bellingham’s improving relationship with Tuchel, which cannot have been harmed by the inclusion of Bellingham’s brother, Jobe, in this squad, is another reason to hope that England still retain the capacity to improve after the World Cup. The elder Bellingham has become England’s most influential player.

England at their best would be one of the few teams capable of extending them. Rice noted on Saturday that the game between the two sides was ‘massive’. England need to prove they can find a way to get closer to the world champions. To beat them, Rice said, would be a ‘massive statement’.

‘Playing against them is a great incentive to win. It will show where we are as a group. We are trying to attack teams full throttle and with players like Harry Kane, Jude Bellingham and Morgan Rogers in our attack, it feels as if it is going to take off one night and maybe tomorrow night will be the night. We can beat Spain. For sure, we can.’.

Industry observers note that tuchel needs to prove England can win, not just be noble contenders. They need to prove that their DNA need not be a curse.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This was the afternoon when Xabi Alonso’s Chelsea went from swashbuckling to stoic, thrilling to tenacious.

For all Alonso’s attacking vigour at the start of his reign, there can have been no more symbolically satisfying victory under the new coach than this resolute win at Everton – the most vivid example of an increasingly impressive transformation.

Industry observers note that this was what Alonso described as “winning in a different way”. A triumph amid the adversity of losing goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez to what appears to be a serious injury after a head collision with Jarrad Branthwaite is just one facet of why the joyous visiting supporters might consider this an early turning point.

Where recently they wilted, on Saturday they thrived in securing a first Premier League clean sheet for nine months.

Much more of this and the adjectives which were splattered across Chelsea during the golden years of José Mourinho – solid, robust and dogged – will be part of the Stamford Bridge lexicon once more.

Sources indicate that “Just one day,” Alonso warned, both acclaiming the importance of the win while wisely preaching caution. “It will be key when we manage 10 clean sheets, even though this one feels good. We need to repeat it again and again, but the mentality was very good. Sometimes it is not to play nice, it is to play good – to win second balls, and to be efficient. We needed one of these: a clean sheet and a win.”.

Sources indicate that asked about Martinez’s condition, Alonso mentioned: “It was a concussion, but beyond that I do not know. I have only seen one clip of the incident, so we need to wait.

“What we know is that he left the stadium conscious and is now in hospital undergoing precautionary tests.

“We need to wait. Hopefully it will not be too serious, but at the moment we just have to wait.”.

Alonso is speedily shifting perceptions of this previously underperforming bunch, the Stamford Bridge culture on and off the pitch already unrecognisable from a few months ago.

It was Chelsea’s trip to Everton last season which facilitated the endgame of Liam Rosenior’s short, but generally hideous reign.

For those who tried to banish memories, it was a darkly comical period when Chelsea’s players were paying their respect to stationary footballs, seemingly finding newly introduced ways to stand in front of travelling fans to apologise for meek and rancid performances.

How different the scenes after Pedro Neto’s double on Merseyside – a success built on those old-fashioned and too often underestimated qualities of character and application before the artists had the final say. These are the wins that build connections and trust between players and supporters, especially during the getting-to-know-you period of a managerial tenure. While neutrals mutter about a generally disappointing spectacle, the players and supporters return home clutching three points believing they have fought together in the trenches.

It cannot be overlooked how this win owed a debt to the erratic refereeing of Paul Tierney, especially the amnesty he offered to Morgan Rogers on the stroke of half-time.

Already booked, Rogers was fortunate not to receive a second caution for a lunge on James Garner which took the man after the ball. A replica challenge by Everton’s Harrison Armstrong had warranted a yellow card in Tierney’s world just 21 minutes earlier.

The home team’s argument that this was a potential game changer was supported when the England midfielder was inevitably involved in the move which led to Neto breaking through 44 seconds into the second half – a lead Chelsea never looked like surrendering as Everton’s attacking limitations were exposed.

Mike Penders deputised for the stricken Martínez – conscious but taken to hospital as a precaution – and was well-protected.

As much as Alonso’s artistry as a midfield maestro is presumed to define him as a coach, one cannot help but believe there are many who underestimate him as a football student. He was never going to return to England clinging to one idea given his previous Premier League experience, and he intuitively knew an away game at Everton was one for foot soldiers.

He signed Jordan Henderson for such a task. Just like his manager, the former Liverpool captain was primed for enemy territory.

Alonso’s anticipation of a fixture in which a battle had to be fought before there was an outbreak of football proved correct, aided by the fussy and generally terrible first-half officiating of Tierney.

In a recent development, alonso’s name has not echoed so loudly across the Mersey since he played a few miles down the road from Everton’s latest home. After several calamitous appointments, those fans can believe their team are in safe hands again.

He is looking to vice captains Moises Caceido and Levi Colwill to step up in his absence, explaining: “You can be a captain without an armband, for sure. Leadership is notable and that’s why we have this group, not just on matchday.”.

James remains vital to Chelsea at their best, and while his minutes have been managed, it’s a huge disappointment to see him need to go under the knife once more.

We have not got too many players. I am not saying we’re going to win the league, but we want to try to challenge and be around the top teams.”.

That might be made harder by the news that the Friedkin Group are already looking to sell the club after only a couple of years in charge. Moyes is a rare thing, a manager who keeps improving despite setbacks, and his second spell has been fairly solid so far.

Moyes is aware that Chelsea pose a threat up front, adding: “Their attacking line is incredibly exciting. I also think they have got some super defenders as well, but they are playing quite an expansive game, which on its day can lead to goals and on another day it can lead to defeats.”.

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Everton vs Chelsea.

According to recent reports, chelsea return to Premier League action this weekend looking to harness the momentum of their emphatic 5-1 victory over Bournemouth before the international break. That Stamford Bridge masterclass ended a frustrating three-match winless streak and was built upon braces from Joao Pedro and Jordan Henderson, alongside another strike from summer signing Morgan Rogers.

Yet the true catalyst for the resurgence was the return of Moises Caicedo. Having shaken off the calf problem that hindered his early-season involvement, the midfielder anchored the side’s win. While defensive vulnerabilities persist - extending an unwanted run of league matches without a clean sheet back to January - the victory offered clear signs of progress under their head coach, Xabi Alonso.

Next up is a notoriously difficult trip to Merseyside to face Everton in Saturday’s lunchtime fixture. Historically, Everton have proven to be a formidable stumbling block for the capital club, particularly on home turf. Everton enter the weekend unbeaten in eight of their last nine home encounters against Chelsea, a stretch that has seen the Londoners fail to score on seven visits and suffer six defeats, including a chastening 3-0 reverse last term that spelt the end for Liam Rosenior.

David Moyes will demand a sharper defensive showing from his side this time around, following a frustrating 2-2 draw with Hull City where a 2-1 lead slipped away. Even so, Everton’s broader defensive record at home offers encouragement, having kept clean sheets in two of their opening three league fixtures at their base.

With both teams eager to build consistency, Saturday’s clash pits Chelsea’s newly found attacking spark against an opponent that traditionally relishes this fixture.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Oliver Thomas | 17 Nov 2026 12:05.

Scotland captain Andrew Robertson has insisted that new head coach Sebastien Pocognoli does not have time to turn their fortunes around after a heavy 4-0 defeat by Switzerland in the UEFA Nations League on Monday.

It was a bitter sweet night for Robertson at Berit Sitterstadion, as he won his 103rd international cap to become Scotland’s all-time record appearance-maker, surpassing Kenny Dalglish’s record that stood for 40 years.

However, Robertson’s personal achievement was soon overshadowed by a disappointing loss to Switzerland which has consigned them to a third-place finish in League B Group 1 of the Nations League.

Against a much-changed Swiss side, Scotland gifted the hosts a 22nd-minute lead when midfielder Lewis Ferguson inadvertently diverted a harmless cross into his own net.

Scotland’s alarming collapse in St Gallen began with two more goals conceded in the first six minutes of the second half, before Zeki Amdouni netted Switzerland’s fourth in the closing stages to rub salt into the visitors’ wounds.

Sources indicate that "I thought first half we were in the game," Robertson told reporters after the match. "We lost a stupid goal but I thought we had chances and could easily have been one-each at half time.

In a recent development, "We talk about it at half time to say keep going and by 50 minutes we're 3-0 down. That cannot happen in international football.

Recent findings suggest that "We were playing against a good team, but we were in the game in the first half. We have to do it for 90 minutes. Then you're 3-0 down at a tough place. A really tough night for us.".

Scotland boss Pocognoli, who was appointed as Steve Clarke's successor in August, has previously called for patience as he attempts to implement an attacking philosophy with the national team.

However, the 39-year-old Belgian has prevailed in only two of his first six games in charge – both against North Macedonia – and the Tartan Army have seen their team concede 10 goals in the process.

According to recent reports, questioned on how long it might take for Pocognoli’s approach to yield positive results, Robertson warned: "I don't think you've got time in international football. You have to do it.

"Are those supporters who have travelled everywhere going to give us time? No. Are the people inside Hampden going to give us time? No.

Sources indicate that “Are the people outside Hampden that are going to be critical, and rightly so, going to give us time? No. We've not got time. The players don't have time. We have to step up.

In a recent development, "We now have a long break until March which is not a good thing. It's going to be a tough one to swallow.".

Having accumulated seven points from six Nations League games, Scotland have missed out on a quarter-final spot but have avoided relegation from League B.

Scotland will therefore have no competitive fixtures during the next international break in March 2027 when Pocognoli will instead prepare for friendly fixtures.

It has been a positive international break for Diego Moreira, who continued his excellent form from club football.

According to recent reports, as La Gazzetta dello Sport write this morning, Ruben Amorim will welcome Moreira back to Milanello soon. The winger has become a regular starter and producing goals and assists, but the Portuguese coach knows the pitfalls of the match against Frosinone all too well.

Therefore, starting Thursday – when the squad will be fully back together after the day off tomorrow – everyone’s minds will be focused solely on the new busy schedule awaiting the Rossoneri until Christmas. More specifically, seven matches from Sunday until December 19th.

In a recent development, immediately after the last international break, the Rossoneri drew away to Sassuolo, a result that certainly wasn’t greeted with a smile. The goal is to avoid repeating that misstep against Alvini’s team, and Moreira will be key to that.

According to recent reports, despite his 22 years of age and the €50m valuation plus bonuses that could have weighed heavily on his shoulders, Diego hasn’t taken long to win over Milan fans. In his last six league matches (he missed two due to injury), he’s scored four goals and provided three assists.

Industry observers note that he has also demonstrated his ability to switch roles with ease, playing as a winger on the right or left, as a wing-back or even as a full-back. He plays with the boldness of someone who targets his opponent and tries to dribble past him, something that fans always appreciate.

Sources indicate that moreira always seeks one-on-one situations, both due to his strengths and the explicit request of Amorim, who asks his wide players to create numerical superiority. Diego is succeeding remarkably, as his assist for Christian Pulisic in the derby shows, as he got past Carlo Augusto and crossed.

Moreira made the difference against Italy on Sunday too: not only did he score the fourth goal, which he celebrated by making a gesture of ‘one, two, three and four’ with his fingers, but he also kept accelerating, hit the woodwork, shot wide once more and had two shots blocked by his opponents.

According to recent reports, he set up De Bruyne for a shot, had more touches than anyone else in the opponents’ area (11) and often took on Calafiori and Dimarco, delighting the crowd with a spectacular backheel. He had around 50 touches and 27/31 completed passes, earning the applause of the entire stadium when he came off.

Moreira is at the moment captivating thanks to his drive and desire. He’s that way at Milan and he’s that way with the national team. That’s why there’s a version of the Rossoneri with him and another without him which, frankly, isn’t as threatening.

In a recent development, amorim carefully integrated him into the team’s operations at the start of the season, but now he has broken the padlock off and now considers him a key player in the team. This doesn’t mean he won’t need a breather, given the schedule, but the coach will have to think about the right moments to rest.

According to recent reports, with four goals in Serie A (one every 121 minutes), he’s already matched his four goals from last season in Ligue 1, and he has no intention of stopping. He feels the confidence in himself and the team.

The leap from Ligue 1 to Serie A didn’t bother him. In fact, he intends to continue dancing on the pitch, just like in the derby or against Italy. On Sunday, he wants to show he has the same energy with which he brought Italy to its knees. Milan and San Siro await him.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Liverpool have been linked with many different players over the years.

However, their last couple have consisted of the most spending that they've ever done.

Around £600 million has been splashed on newly introduced players by Liverpool and, there are still a lot more areas among their ranks that could do with an upgrade or two.

Right now, it's unclear what their main priorities are but, since they're fourth in the Premier League and find themselves nine points adrift of first-placed Arsenal, it's clear that change is needed.

Obviously, big deals don't often get completed in January but, if Iraola wants to give his men the best chance possible this term, some big transfers are going to have to be agreed.

Liverpool are eyeing up a move for Josko Gvardiol.

Right now, left-back is probably one of Liverpool's main problem areas.

Milos Kerkez and Kostas Tsimikas have both failed to meet expectations with neither of them managing to prove their worth.

Of course, the former of the two is still young so he still has a lot of his career ahead of him but, since he's their first choice, you'd have expected a lot more from him.

Links with left-backs such as Alejandro Balde and Julian Ryerson have emerged but, thanks to an update from El Nacional CAT, an even better option has entered the discussion.

"Barcelona are calmly considering the possibility of trying to sign Gvardiol, although this would involve a significant investment," they wrote.

"The Sky Blues won't let go of a player for whom they paid over €90 million, making him one of the most expensive defenders of all time. Nor will they allow him to leave mid-season, so they would have to wait until the summer transfer window.

"Furthermore, there is another obstacle that makes it extremely difficult to see the former Dinamo Zagreb and RB Leipzig player at the Spotify Camp Nou, and for him to be available to Hans-Dieter Flick.

"There will be a lot of competition for Gvardiol The situation surrounding Gvardiol and City has attracted the attention of many clubs , who are willing to try their luck and fight for his signing.

"For example, he has been linked with Paris Saint-Germain, Liverpool, Bayern Munich, Chelsea, and Al-Nassr. In other words, Barça will face several rivals in the fight to secure his services.".

Josko Gvardiol's dream move has always been Liverpool.

Before Manchester City jumped in and prised Josko Gvardiol away from RB Leipzig, the Croatian always spoke about how it was his dream to join Liverpool.

There have been several interviews where the "incredible" defender has shared that the team he supports is Liverpool.

His favoured position is obviously centre-back but, with the Reds still having now idea what they're doing with that area of their squad, he could come in as another option at left-back for Liverpool.

Not only would this help shore up Iraola's defence like Ronald Araujo has but, it would also give Kerkez someone to properly compete against.

Of course, the window isn't open yet so deals can't be struck right now but, the fact that Gvardiol has re-entered Liverpool's thinking is excellent news.

Published: 13:01 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 20:45 EST, 14 November 2026.

A former Premier League referee was mistakenly declared dead by football chiefs this week.

On Tuesday, the Football Association of Wales (FAW) announced Keith Cooper had died aged 78. But he is alive and well.

The news reached the ears of the Wembley Cup final referee when he went out to his local sports centre for a flu jab only to be told: 'You were dead.'.

The Football Association of Wales posted a statement online and a tribute on social media to announce his death, but then withdrew it within an hour.

Mr Cooper, who is the father of former Nottingham Forest and Leicester boss Steve Cooper, told a Welsh sports website: 'I walked into the sports centre yesterday to have my jab and the fellow went, "You were dead!".

'Well, I'm not dead, I'm here and I'm OK!'.

The blunder appears to have emerged after the Wiltshire FA announced the death of another referee called Keith Cooper, who the football chiefs in Wales believed was the other Keith Cooper.

The FAW statement said: 'Keith was a well-known figure who enjoyed an exceptional career at both domestic and international level and would later hold the position of FAW Referees' Officer following his retirement in 1996.

On Tuesday, the Football Association of Wales (FAW) announced Keith Cooper had died aged 78.

'Born and raised in Pontypridd, he is considered one of Wales' best match officials through his highly-regarded status in the game.

'In addition to his work with FAW, Keith was also a valued member of the Wiltshire FA Council who recognised his 'integrity, passion and commitment' in their tribute to his services to the game.

'Everyone at the FAW sends their condolences to his family and friends at this sad time.'.

Mr Cooper oversaw the 1994 League Cup final between Aston Villa and Manchester United, won by Villa 3-1, and worked in radio punditry after hanging up his whistle.

Recent findings suggest that the FAW has not issued an explanation over the posted tribute. His family has not yet commented on the error.

But the unfortunate mistake has not spared the FAW from ridicule by other football fans.

The 26-year-old was allegedly targeted by Premier League champions Arsenal who were keen to explore a big-money move for the left-sided attacker as he approached the final 12 months of his contract.

However, a transfer to the Emirates Stadium failed to materialise and Vinicius opted to sign a upcoming long-term contract at Real Madrid in August, keeping him at the Bernabeu until 2032.

Speculation over his future in the Spanish capital intensified shortly after Brazil's disappointing last-16 exit at the 2026 World Cup, which led to him not training as much as he should have by his own admission.

Under latest Real Madrid boss Jose Mourinho, Vinicius has been unable to reach the heights expected on a consistent basis, scoring just one goal and registering three assists in 12 appearances across all competitions this season.

Vinicius has since opened up on how a summer of speculation and an early World Cup exit has contributed to his drop-off in form at club level.

“I don’t think I prepared as well as I could have after the World Cup because the impact of that tournament is so significant for all Brazilians,” Vinicius remarked at a press conference in Singapore ahead of Brazil’s friendly on Tuesday.

“Being knocked out so early was something we hadn’t expected, so I took advantage of my holidays to enjoy myself, rest, relax, and spend more time with my family.

Sources indicate that “I ended up training less than in previous years. That may have affected my start to the season.

“On ‌top of that, regarding my contract renewal, with so many clubs showing interest last summer, I felt truly overwhelmed, as with the situation at Real Madrid, but it’s a very long season.”.

In October, Vinicius was handed a straight red card and a four-match suspension after pulling the hair of Villarreal midfielder Nathan Saliba.

Real Madrid’s club-record signing Yan Diomande has since flourished for Mourinho’s side in Vinicius’s preferred left-sided position, and the Brazilian has acknowledged that he has work to do to win back his place in the starting lineup.

“Maintaining such a high level for so long is always very difficult,” Real’s No.7 added.

In a recent development, “I think only Cristiano Ronaldo and [Lionel] Messi have managed to do this for so many years, reaching the same kinds of numbers. I am human, I often make mistakes, but I always try to improve.”.

Since joining Real Madrid from Flamengo in 2018, Vinicius has played 387 times for the club across all competitions, recording 129 goals and 103 assists as well as winning three La Liga titles and two Champions Leagues.

Mourinho recently stated that he is confident that Vinicius will rediscover his top form with the Spanish giants in the not too distant future.
